topics.title: Meaning of Marginal Cost & Marginal Costing
explain: Marginal cost is the change in total cost when one extra unit of product is produced.
It equals the aggregate of prime costs and variable overheads.
Marginal costing values products and inventory at variable costs only.
Fixed costs are treated as period costs and charged to Profit and Loss.
Incremental cost represents total cost change from altering production volume or processes.

flow.title: Calculation of Marginal Cost
steps: Identify direct materials cost
Identify direct labour cost
Identify variable overheads
Sum prime cost and variable overheads
Result is total marginal cost

topics.example: If producing 10 notebooks costs ₹10,000 and 11 notebooks costs ₹10,500, the marginal cost of the 11th unit is ₹500.
remember: Marginal Cost = Prime Cost + Variable Overheads.
Fixed costs remain constant irrespective of minor changes in volume.
mistakes: Confusing unit-level marginal cost with batch-level setup cost changes.

quiz.q: What constitutes marginal cost in cost accounting?
quiz.why: Marginal cost is precisely the sum of prime cost and variable overheads.

quiz.q: Under marginal costing, how are products and inventories valued?
quiz.why: Marginal costing values products and stock using variable costs only.

topics.title: Characteristics of Marginal Costing
explain: All costs are segregated strictly into fixed and variable elements.
Semi-variable costs are divided into their fixed and variable parts.
Only variable costs are treated as product or inventoriable costs.
Finished goods and WIP exclude fixed manufacturing overheads.
Fixed costs are written off as period costs in the period incurred.

flow.title: Cost Treatment under Marginal Costing
steps: Classify total cost into fixed and variable
Separate semi-variable costs into fixed and variable
Assign variable costs to product inventory
Charge fixed costs to Profit and Loss
Determine product profitability using contribution

topics.example: Factory rent is charged as a period expense in full, while raw fabric cost is assigned to garment inventory.
remember: Fixed costs are period costs, never inventoriable costs in marginal costing.
Selling prices are evaluated using contribution margin.
mistakes: Including variable selling expenses when valuing closing inventory.

quiz.q: Which of the following is treated as a period cost under marginal costing?
quiz.why: Fixed costs are treated as period costs and charged directly to profit and loss.

quiz.q: Inventory valuation under marginal costing excludes which cost?
quiz.why: Fixed manufacturing costs are excluded from closing stock valuation under marginal costing.

topics.title: Determination of Cost, Contribution, and Profit
explain: Contribution is the excess of Sales Revenue over Total Variable Costs.
Contribution forms a fund to recover fixed expenses and generate profit.
Product Contribution Margin equals Sales minus Variable Manufacturing Costs.
Profit is derived by deducting total Fixed Costs from Contribution.
If Contribution equals Fixed Costs, the entity operates at zero profit or loss.

flow.title: Marginal Costing Income Statement Flow
steps: Start with Sales Revenue
Deduct Variable Manufacturing Costs
Obtain Product Contribution Margin
Deduct Variable Non-Manufacturing Costs
Obtain Total Contribution
Deduct Total Fixed Costs for Profit

topics.example: If Sales are ₹80,000, Variable Costs are ₹50,000, and Fixed Costs are ₹20,000, Contribution is ₹30,000 and Profit is ₹10,000.
remember: Contribution (C) = Sales Revenue (S) - Variable Costs (V).
Profit = Contribution - Fixed Costs.
mistakes: Subtracting fixed costs before computing contribution margin.

quiz.q: What is the basic equation for Contribution?
quiz.why: Contribution is defined as Sales Revenue minus Total Variable Costs.

quiz.q: When Contribution exceeds Fixed Costs, the result is:
quiz.why: Excess of contribution over fixed costs represents profit.

topics.title: Absorption Costing vs Marginal Costing
explain: Absorption costing assigns both fixed and variable costs to products.
Marginal costing assigns only variable costs to products.
When production exceeds sales, absorption costing shows higher profit due to fixed costs carried in closing stock.
When sales exceed production, marginal costing shows higher profit.
Profit difference equals fixed overhead rate multiplied by change in stock volume.

flow.title: Profit Comparison based on Inventory Levels
steps: Compare production quantity with sales quantity
If production > sales, absorption profit is higher
If sales > production, marginal profit is higher
If production = sales, both profits are equal

topics.example: If 220 units are produced and 160 sold, absorption costing carries forward fixed costs of 60 unsold units into stock.
remember: Difference in profit = (Closing Stock - Opening Stock) × Fixed Overhead Absorption Rate.
Both methods yield identical profit when opening stock equals closing stock.
mistakes: Assuming absorption costing always shows lower profit than marginal costing regardless of stock changes.

quiz.q: If production is greater than sales in a period, profit under absorption costing will be:
quiz.why: Absorption costing defers a portion of fixed overheads in closing stock when production > sales.

quiz.q: Under absorption costing, fixed manufacturing costs are treated as:
quiz.why: Absorption costing absorbs fixed manufacturing costs into product cost.

topics.title: Advantages and Limitations of Marginal Costing
explain: Advantage: Prevents over- or under-absorption of fixed overheads.
Advantage: Provides a simple basis for short-term pricing and decision making.
Advantage: Prevents distortion of periodic profits by fixed cost deferral.
Limitation: Classifying all costs strictly into fixed and variable is difficult.
Limitation: Ignores the time factor and heavy investment required for long jobs.

flow.title: Evaluating Marginal Costing Utility
steps: Segregate costs into fixed and variable
Evaluate contribution per unit for quick pricing
Avoid carrying fixed costs in inventory
Acknowledge limitation of cost classification
Consider key limiting factors for decisions

topics.example: A manager accepts a special order at ₹15 per unit when variable cost is ₹10, even if total absorption cost was ₹18.
remember: Marginal costing is a managerial technique, not an independent costing method.
WIP and closing stock are understated as fixed overheads are omitted.
mistakes: Using marginal cost pricing for regular long-term sales without recovering fixed costs.

quiz.q: Which problem of absorption costing is eliminated by marginal costing?
quiz.why: Fixed costs are written off as period costs, avoiding under or over-absorption.

quiz.q: A major limitation of marginal costing is that it:
quiz.why: Marginal costing ignores the time taken and capital investment involved in completing jobs.

topics.title: Cost-Volume-Profit (CVP) Analysis & Assumptions
explain: CVP analysis studies relationships between costs, sales volume, and profit.
Assumes output volume is the sole driver of revenue and cost changes.
Assumes total costs split linearly into static fixed and proportional variable costs.
Assumes selling price, unit variable cost, and fixed costs remain constant.
Assumes time value of money is ignored.

flow.title: Steps in CVP Analysis
steps: Identify unit selling price and variable cost
Determine total fixed costs for relevant range
Calculate contribution per unit
Estimate profit or loss at target sales volumes

topics.example: A firm calculates how many units to sell at ₹300 to cover ₹3,00,000 fixed overheads when variable cost is ₹285.
remember: CVP assumes linear behavior for total costs and total revenues.
Product mix proportion remains constant in multi-product CVP analysis.
mistakes: Assuming unit variable cost changes as total volume increases within the relevant range.

quiz.q: Which assumption underpins Cost-Volume-Profit analysis?
o: Fixed costs vary with output level
Total revenues and costs are linear within relevant range
Selling price per unit decreases with volume
Time value of money is factored in
quiz.why: CVP assumes total revenues and total costs behave linearly in the relevant range.

quiz.q: In CVP analysis, what is assumed about the sales mix for multiple products?
quiz.why: CVP assumes the proportion of sales among different products stays constant.

topics.title: Marginal Cost Equation & Profit-Volume (P/V) Ratio
explain: Marginal Cost Equation: Sales - Variable Cost = Contribution = Fixed Cost ± Profit.
Profit-Volume (P/V) Ratio shows the proportion of sales available to cover fixed cost and profit.
Formula: P/V Ratio = (Contribution / Sales) × 100.
Alternative Formula: P/V Ratio = (Change in Profit or Contribution / Change in Sales) × 100.
Higher P/V ratio implies faster profit growth after reaching break-even.

flow.title: P/V Ratio Derivation Flow
steps: Subtract unit variable cost from selling price
Obtain unit contribution
Divide unit contribution by unit selling price
Multiply by 100 to express as percentage

topics.example: If selling price is ₹30 and variable cost is ₹15, Contribution is ₹15, giving a P/V Ratio of (15/30) × 100 = 50%.
remember: P/V Ratio + Variable Cost Ratio = 100%.
Contribution = Sales × P/V Ratio.
mistakes: Using net profit instead of contribution in the P/V ratio formula numerator.

quiz.q: If Sales are ₹1,00,000 and Variable Costs are ₹60,000, what is the P/V Ratio?
If selling price per unit increases while unit variable cost remains unchanged, the P/V ratio will:
quiz.why: Increasing selling price increases contribution per unit, thereby raising the P/V ratio.

topics.title: Break-Even Point (BEP), Cash BEP & Multi-Product BEP
explain: Break-Even Point (BEP) is the sales volume where total costs equal total revenue (zero profit/loss).
BEP (in units) = Fixed Costs / Contribution per unit.
BEP (in Value) = Fixed Costs / P/V Ratio.
Cash BEP considers only cash fixed costs, excluding non-cash items like depreciation.
Multi-product BEP uses weighted composite contribution based on sales mix.

flow.title: Calculating Composite Break-Even Point
steps: Identify sales mix proportion of each product
Calculate contribution per unit for each product
Compute weighted composite contribution per unit
Divide common fixed cost by composite contribution
Apportion total BEP units into products using mix ratio

topics.example: If fixed costs are ₹2,00,000 and contribution per unit is ₹200, BEP = 2,00,000 / 200 = 1,000 units.
remember: Cash BEP = Cash Fixed Costs / Contribution per unit.
At BEP, Total Contribution = Total Fixed Costs.
mistakes: Including depreciation when calculating Cash Break-Even Point.

quiz.q: What is the break-even point in units if Fixed Cost is ₹1,50,000 and Contribution per unit is ₹15?
quiz.why: BEP in units = Fixed Cost / Contribution per unit = 1,50,000 / 15 = 10,000 units.

quiz.q: Cash Break-Even Point excludes which of the following from fixed cost?
quiz.why: Cash BEP excludes non-cash expenses such as depreciation from fixed costs.

topics.title: Graphical Presentations (BEP Chart, Contribution Chart & P/V Chart)
explain: Break-even Chart plots total cost line and sales line against activity level.
Intersection of total cost line and sales revenue line marks the Break-Even Point.
Contribution Break-even Chart plots variable cost line first, adding fixed costs on top.
Profit-Volume (P/V) Chart plots profit/loss on Y-axis against sales volume on X-axis.
P/V line starts at negative fixed cost at zero activity and cuts X-axis at BEP.

flow.title: Plotting a Profit-Volume (P/V) Graph
steps: Mark loss equal to fixed cost at zero activity on Y-axis
Calculate profit at projected maximum sales volume
Plot the profit point on graph
Draw a straight line connecting loss point and profit point
Locate BEP where line crosses X-axis (zero profit)

topics.example: In a P/V chart with ₹3,00,000 fixed costs, the plot starts at -₹3,00,000 on the Y-axis and climbs past zero at BEP.
remember: BEP is the intersection of the total cost line and total sales line.
P/V chart visually displays profit variations resulting from volume changes.
mistakes: Starting the total cost line from origin instead of the fixed cost intercept on the Y-axis.

quiz.q: On a standard break-even chart, the point where the sales revenue line intersects the total cost line is:
quiz.why: The intersection of total cost line and sales revenue line defines the break-even point.

quiz.q: Where does the line on a Profit-Volume (P/V) chart intersect the horizontal axis?
quiz.why: The horizontal axis represents zero profit/loss, which corresponds to the break-even point.

topics.title: Margin of Safety (MOS) & Angle of Incidence
explain: Margin of Safety (MOS) is the excess of actual or projected sales over break-even sales.
Formula: MOS = Total Sales - Break-Even Sales.
MOS (in value) can also be calculated as Profit / P/V Ratio.
Angle of Incidence is formed by the intersection of sales line and total cost line at BEP.
A wider angle of incidence indicates a higher rate of profit earning after BEP.

flow.title: Calculating Margin of Safety
steps: Determine total actual or budgeted sales
Calculate break-even sales level
Subtract break-even sales from total sales
Divide profit by P/V ratio as alternative validation

topics.example: If projected sales are 1,700 units and break-even sales are 1,000 units, Margin of Safety is 700 units (41.18%).
remember: Margin of Safety = Profit / P/V Ratio.
High MOS + wide angle of incidence = strong, safe profitability position.
mistakes: Confusing Margin of Safety with Break-Even Sales value.

quiz.q: How can Margin of Safety be calculated using profit and P/V ratio?
quiz.why: Margin of Safety (value) = Profit / P/V Ratio.

quiz.q: A large Angle of Incidence together with a high Margin of Safety indicates:
quiz.why: A wide angle means rapid profit generation after BEP, which combined with high MOS indicates strong profitability.

topics.title: Framework & Relevant Costs for Decision Making
explain: Decision making framework: Identify Problem -> Identify Options -> Evaluate Options -> Select Best Option.
A cost is relevant if it is a future cost and differs between alternative options.
Controllable costs are costs directly affected by management's choice.
Sunk costs and historical costs are past costs and always irrelevant for decision making.
Opportunity cost is the benefit forgone by adopting one option over the best alternative.

flow.title: Evaluating Relevance of a Cost
steps: Check if cost will occur in the future
If past cost, treat as sunk and irrelevant
Check if cost differs between choices
If cost is identical for all choices, treat as irrelevant
Include only future differential costs

topics.example: The book value of an old machine is a sunk cost (irrelevant), but its current scrap sale value forgone is an opportunity cost (relevant).
remember: Sunk costs (e.g., past blueprint costs) are never relevant.
Opportunity costs are always relevant when choosing between mutually exclusive options.
mistakes: Including allocated committed fixed costs in decision-making incremental evaluation.

quiz.q: Which type of cost is always irrelevant in short-term managerial decision making?
quiz.why: Sunk costs are historical costs already incurred and cannot be changed by future decisions.

quiz.q: Opportunity cost is defined as:
o: Total fixed cost incurred in past
Potential benefit forgone from next best alternative
quiz.why: Opportunity cost represents the forgone benefit from the best rejected course of action.

topics.title: Short-Term Decision Making & Limiting Factors
explain: Short-term decisions address temporary gaps between demand and supply of resources.
A Limiting (Key) Factor is any factor that restricts the activity level of an entity.
Key factors can be materials, labour hours, machine capacity, or market demand.
When a limiting factor exists, rank products by Contribution per Unit of Limiting Factor.
Profitability ratio under key factor constraint = Contribution / Key Factor unit.

flow.title: Decision Making under Limiting Factor
steps: Identify the constrained resource (key factor)
Calculate contribution per unit for each product
Calculate contribution per unit of limiting factor
Rank products in descending order of contribution per key factor
Allocate available resource to highest ranked products first

topics.example: If Machine P hours are limited, select Product Q over Product P because Q generates ₹16 contribution per machine hour compared to ₹8.50 for P.
remember: Always maximize Contribution per Unit of Limiting Factor.
Optimal product mix gives maximum total contribution within resource constraints.
mistakes: Ranking products based on contribution per unit instead of contribution per unit of limiting factor.

quiz.q: When machine hours are limited, products should be prioritized based on:
quiz.why: When a resource is limited, production is optimized by maximizing contribution per unit of that key factor.

quiz.q: What is a key factor in cost accounting?
o: A factor that limits the volume of output or sales
The total fixed cost of the company
quiz.why: A key (limiting) factor is any resource or constraint that restricts an entity's activity.
